title: Cleansing After Contact with Death
overview: This chapter sets up a special water made from the ashes of a red cow, used to make people ritually clean again after they have touched a dead body.

parts.label: Choosing the red cow (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The people were to bring a young red cow with no flaws that had never worn a yoke for farm work. The text does not explain why it had to be red or unused, and readers have offered different guesses, so no one knows for sure.

parts.label: Burning it outside the camp (vv. 3-6)
parts.note: Eleazar, Aaron's son and the priest next in rank, oversaw its killing outside the camp and sprinkled its blood seven times toward the tent where Israel worshiped, tying the act to God's presence. The whole animal was burned with cedar wood, hyssop (a small bushy plant) and red wool, the same items used to cleanse someone healed of a skin disease.

parts.label: Ashes kept for everyone (vv. 7-10)
parts.note: The ashes were stored in a clean place for the whole community, foreigners living among them included. Oddly, everyone who handled them became ritually unclean, meaning barred from worship, until evening, and even ancient Jewish teachers called this a puzzle.

parts.label: Touching death (vv. 11-16)
parts.note: Touching a corpse, a human bone or a grave, or being in a tent where someone died, made a person unclean for seven days, and even open jars in that tent were affected. One common reading is that death stood opposite to God as the source of life and had to be kept apart from worship; some also see practical benefits like quick burial, though the text does not say so.

parts.label: Using the cleansing water (vv. 17-22)
parts.note: The ashes were mixed with fresh running water, and a clean person sprinkled it with hyssop on the unclean on the third and seventh days, after which they washed and were clean by evening. Refusing was serious, because it polluted the place of worship and the person was "cut off," removed from the community in some way scholars still debate.

disagreement: Christians differ on how much of this rite should be read as pointing to Jesus, since the New Testament book of Hebrews compares the heifer's ashes and suffering "outside the camp" to his death, while others treat the chapter mainly as ancient Israel's purity law with only that broad link.
think: Many cultures mark contact with death through washing, waiting or ritual. What do you think people need after they have been close to someone's death?
